the distinctiveness of stimulus representations is a critical component of drug action, and that the effects of morphines on the distinctiveness of representations can be assessed using the differential serial conditioning procedure.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of morphinomimetic compounds on the processes of stimulus generalization and stimulus memory.
the effects of morphing on the acquisition and expression of conditioned and unconditioned responses.
the effects of drugs on the acquisition, retention, and expression of learned behaviors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data from this study support the hypothesis that morphine, by attenuating the distinctiveness and/or persistence of stimulus representations, can operate to disrupt the acquisition and/or expression of conditioned behavior.
morphine, as a general rule, attenuates the distinctiveness and short-term memory of stimulus representations.

the data of these experiments support the notion that the effects of morphines are due to its ability to disrupt the distinctiveness and/or persistence of the stimulus representation of a conditioned stimulus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

morphine's effects are not limited to a simple reduction in the excitability of the NMR, but rather, morphine can also alter the representation of the conditioned stimulus (CS) by attenuating the distinctiveness of the CS and its short-term persistence.
the effects of morphines on differential classical conditioning and reflex modification are consistent with a model in which morphine operates to reduce stimulus distinctiveness and persistence.
morphine's effects appear to be due to its ability to attenuate the distinctness of stimulus representations, which in turn results in a general attenuation of the conditioned response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
morphine, by altering the persistence and distinctiveness of stimulus representations, may be able to disrupt the acquisition and/or maintenance of drug-seeking behaviors.
, at the doses used, morphine can operate to reduce the distinctiveness and memory for the components of a compound stimulus, but not the distinctiveness of the compound as a whole.

, in addition to the effects of morphin on the unconditioned response (UR) and the unconditioned stimulus (UCS), morphine can operate to attenuate the discriminability of stimuli, the distinctiveness of stimulus representations, and the time course of the conditioned response (CR).
